title: Carried in on a priest's shoulders
hookLine: a singer carried into the temple looks at the Lord from the feet up
carry: start at the feet: god's feet are refuge
tomorrow: a month with no ghee, no milk. what do the girls lean on?
last: LET ME LIE AS A STEP.

lines: CARRIED IN ON A PRIEST'S SHOULDERS.
cards: Feet first. In the old custom of greeting an elder by touching their feet, the hand reaches down before the eyes ever meet. One Alvar's hymn runs on that same instinct.
Tradition says its singer, Tiruppan, came from a community of bards kept outside the temple at Srirangam, and sang to the Lord from the riverbank.
And it says a priest, Lokasaranga, was told by the Lord himself to carry the singer inside on his own shoulders. He did.

teach.b: The hymn is short, named by its opening words, Amalanadipiran: the spotless one, the first Lord. What's remarkable is its path.

Tiruppan stands before the image of Vishnu reclining at Srirangam, and he doesn't take it all in at once. He looks the way a devotee bows, starting at the feet. The holy feet, he sings, have come into my eyes.

teach.h: THE GAZE BEGINS AT THE FEET.
teach.b: In Sri Vaishnava prayer the Lord's feet are the refuge itself: the dvaya, one of the tradition's holiest prayers, takes refuge at Narayana's feet.
It's also why Hindus touch an elder's feet: you begin low, and ask blessing there. Then his gaze rises, one verse at a time. The red cloth at the waist.
The navel, where the lotus of Brahma grows. The chest, where the goddess Lakshmi dwells. The throat.
The red mouth. The long, wide eyes. And then the whole dark, beautiful form at once.
Each part reminds him of a story, like the throat that once swallowed the worlds. Then the last verse turns, and it's the line people remember.
Having seen my nectar, he says, these eyes of mine will not look at anything else. The tradition says that with this song he merged into the Lord. Notice who sings it.
A man kept outside the walls is carried in, and sings the hymn the temple keeps. Two days ago the Narada Bhakti Sutras said there is no distinction among those who love, because they are his.
Here, on a priest's shoulders, is that line acted out.

how: In Sri Vaishnava tradition, Tiruppan Alvar's Amalanadipiran is recited in daily worship, and devotees are taught to behold the deity in the temple from the feet upward.

Lokasaranga, told by the Lord, carried him in on his shoulders.

games.q: you're Tiruppan, carried inside at last and standing before the Lord at Srirangam. where does your song begin?
games.why: the hymn begins with the holy feet coming into his eyes, then rises through the waist, chest, throat and mouth to the eyes.

practice: Choose something in front of you, an image you hold sacred if you have one, or a plant, or a face in a photo, and look only at the bottom of it for a breath or two.
Then let the eyes rise a little at a time, staying with each part, and only at the top take it all in at once and rest there. If you pray, you can let this be a way of beholding God.

wordCard.voice: The Alvar hymns. In Tiruppan's Amalanadipiran, a gaze that rises from the Lord's feet to his eyes and then won't look at anything else.

orig.note: Tamil āḻvār: the name the tradition explains as one sunk deep in God; Tiruppan is one of the Alvars.

carryVoice: Your line: start at the feet: God's feet are refuge. Tiruppan began there, and was carried in. See you tomorrow.
